full_text: The bear is the only animal related to man, the Sámi say. Half of all preserved Sámi drums bear the image of the bear, its power invoked for hunting and healing. When a bear was killed, the entire camp participated in a ceremony that could last for days. The 48-part bear yoik, recorded in 1775, reenacts every stage of the hunt and the celebration. First, the hunters track the bear to its den, where the Ulda's old mother has been feeding it all winter. The bear is awakened and killed with respect, for it has given itself to the hunters. Its body is carried to the camp in a procession, with the bear's head facing forward so it can see where it is going. The bear is addressed directly in song: 'You are our guest, you are our relative.' A feast is held, and specific parts of the bear are distributed according to ancient rules. The bear participated symbolically in its own feast, its spirit honored and thanked. After the feast, the bear's bones are buried in a specific pattern, pointed east toward the sunrise, so that the bear can be reborn. The bear came from the sky, lowered in a cradle on a silver and gold chain by God himself, and the ceremony ensures he returns there to be born again.
moral: The bear is a relative, not a quarry; killing him requires honor, respect, and gratitude.
source: laits.utexas.edu (The Bear Went Down the Mountain); MDPI Religions 2021

title: The Bäckahästen – The Brook Horse of Åland's Waters
summary: The bäckahästen (brook horse) is a shapeshifting water spirit that appears as a beautiful, seemingly tame horse near streams, lakes, or the sea. When someone climbs onto its back, the horse gallops into the water and drowns its rider. The legend was particularly used to warn children away from dangerous waters. In some versions, the bäckahästen can be tricked by throwing a piece of steel or iron over its head, forcing it to revert to its true form. This creature overlaps with the Näcken tradition and is closely related to the Celtic kelpie. The countless inlets, streams, and shallow coastal waters of the Åland archipelago made this a particularly relevant cautionary tale for island children. The creature appears numerous times in the Sagenkartan entries from the Swedish-speaking regions of Finland.
full_text:
The bäckahästen is a shapeshifting water spirit that appears as a beautiful, seemingly tame horse near streams, lakes, or the sea — its coat gleaming, its mane flowing like water, its eyes dark and knowing. When someone climbs onto its back, the horse gallops toward the water with unnatural speed, ignoring all attempts to rein it in. By the time the rider realizes what is happening, they are already submerged, dragged beneath the surface by a creature that has been luring humans to their deaths since before memory.

The legend was particularly used to warn children away from dangerous waters, and in many families the threat of the bäckahästen was as effective as any parental command. In some versions, the bäckahästen can be tricked by throwing a piece of steel or iron over its head, forcing it to revert to its true form — a writhing, dark shape that sinks into the depths.

This creature overlaps with the Näcken tradition and is closely related to the Celtic kelpie, a water horse of Scottish and Irish folklore. The countless inlets, streams, and shallow coastal waters of the Åland archipelago made this a particularly relevant cautionary tale for island children, who grew up surrounded by water on every side. The creature appears numerous times in the Sagenkartan entries from the Swedish-speaking regions of Finland, a testament to the enduring power of this terrifying figure.

title: The Birth of Changing Woman
summary: In the Navajo tradition, Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé) was the first human born in the Fourth World. She was originally born as Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́ (White Shell Girl) and matured into Changing Woman, a central deity who represents the cycles of life, the seasons, and the earth itself. She later gives birth to the Hero Twins, Monster Slayer (Naayééʼ Neizghání) and Child of the Water (Tóbájíshchíní), who defeat the monsters plaguing the Navajo people. Changing Woman eventually departs to live in the west, where she resides in a floating house made of turquoise and abalone, creating the seasons as she ages and rejuvenates each year.
source: Diné Bahaneʼ; Washington Matthews, Navaho Legends (1897); Aileen O'Bryan, The Diné: Origin Myths of the Navajo Indians (1956)
full_text:
When the Holy People emerged into the Fourth World, they found it vast and empty, the land stretching in every direction beneath a sky that had no sun. Among them walked White Shell Girl — Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́ — born in the Third World from the foam of sacred waters and the breath of First Man. She was quiet where others were loud, still where others moved, and the Holy People sometimes forgot she was there.

But the Sun did not forget.

Turquoise Boy — Jóhonaa'éí — watched her from the place where the sun would eventually rise. He loved her from a distance, sending rays of light that warmed her skin and made the white shell of her body glow. When he finally came to her in the form of a handsome young man wrapped in light, she did not flinch. They spent four days together, and when he departed at dawn, she knew she carried new life within her.

The months passed slowly. Changing Woman — for that is what she was becoming — walked among the people, and her belly grew round as the full moon. On the day of her delivery, the earth shook. She gave birth to two boys, each emerging from different sides of her body. The first was Naayéé' Neizghání — Monster Slayer — born from her right side, his fists already clenched around bolts of lightning. The second was Tóbájíshchíní — Child of the Water — born from her left, his eyes reflecting the depth of every lake and river.

The twins grew with unnatural speed. Within days they were walking, within weeks they were men, and within months they had set out to destroy the monsters — the anaye — that had been devouring the people since the time of the separation. They killed Yéʼiitsoh, the Big Giant, and Déélgééd the Horned Monster, and all the others who had made the Fourth World a place of terror.

After the monsters fell, Changing Woman grew old. Her skin wrinkled, her hair turned white, and she knew her time in the physical world was ending. But she made a promise: each year, as winter approached, she would age further, until she became nothing but memory. And each spring, when the first warm wind blew from the west, she would be young again.

She built a floating house of turquoise and abalone shell on an island in the western ocean and departed from the shore in a boat of light. The people watched her go. And every year since, when the leaves turn gold and fall, the Navajo know it is Changing Woman growing old. And when the first green shoots push through the soil in spring, they know she has been born again.

title: Big Water Creature and the Great Flood
summary: In the Third World, after the reunion of men and women, a mother and her two daughters missed the raft crossing and swam the river. Big Water Creature (Tééhoołtsódii) seized the daughters and dragged them underwater. Talking God and Water Sprinkler created bowls of white and blue shell that spun an opening to an underwater house. First Man and First Woman rescued the girls while Coyote (First Angry) stole Big Water Creature's own two children. In retaliation, Big Water Creature sent a great flood from all directions. The people fled to the sacred mountain Sisnaajiní, where First Man planted the Male Reed. Woodpecker hollowed the reed, and the people climbed into the Fourth World through its passage, just ahead of the rising waters.
source: Diné Bahaneʼ; Aileen O'Bryan, The Diné: Origin Myths of the Navajo Indians (1956)
full_text:
After the men and women reunited, they began crossing the river on rafts of bundled reeds, ferrying people and possessions to the south bank where the sacred mountains waited. One mother and her two daughters missed the last crossing. The sun was going down, and the river was rising.

The women waded in. The water was cold, colder than any water should be, and it pulled at them with hands they could not see. Midway across, something seized the two daughters — Big Water Creature, Tééhoołtsódii, the great spirit of the deep water. He dragged them under. The mother screamed and clawed at the surface, but the girls were gone.

Talking God and Water Sprinkler came to the riverbank. They created two bowls — one of white shell, one of blue — and set them spinning on the water's surface. The spinning bowls bored a hole through the river's skin, revealing an underwater house where Big Water Creature kept his captive children in a dark pool.

First Man and First Woman dove through the opening and rescued the girls. But while they were below, Coyote — First Angry — crept into Big Water Creature's house and stole the creature's own two children, hiding them under his robe.

When Big Water Creature discovered his children gone, he flew into a rage that shook the earth. He called water from every direction — from the springs, from the clouds, from the frozen peaks of the north. The river rose. The plains flooded. Water poured through the valleys like a wall.

The people ran to Sisnaajiní, the Sacred Mountain in the East, its peak white with shell and lightning. They climbed to the top as the water lapped at their feet. First Man planted the Male Reed — a hollow stalk as tall as a man — and called to Woodpecker. Woodpecker hollowed the reed with his beak, drilling a passage from the bottom to the top.

The people climbed inside. They could hear the water rising outside, could feel the reed swaying. One by one, they crawled upward through the hollow stem — First Man, First Woman, the Holy People, and even Coyote with the stolen children still under his arm. They emerged into the Fourth World, gasping in the light, just ahead of the flood that pursued them like a living thing.

Behind them, the Third World drowned. But it was not destroyed — it lives still beneath the waters, a place where the Holy People sometimes return in dreams.

title: The Boy Who Crossed the Great Water and Returned
summary: A Hopi tale of a boy who journeyed across the great waters and returned with knowledge and power. The boy's curiosity led him to leave his village and travel east toward the rising sun. He encountered various supernatural beings and overcame trials, including crossing a body of water that no Hopi had crossed before. Guided by Spider Grandmother, he learned sacred songs and ceremonies from the spirits on the other side. When he returned to his people, he brought new ceremonies, dance forms, and agricultural knowledge that benefited the Hopi. The story reflects the Hopi belief that spiritual power and knowledge can be gained through journeys to sacred places and that those who venture forth with pure hearts return to enrich the community.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993)
full_text:
The boy's name has been lost, which is fitting, because the story is not about who he was but about what he found. He lived in a village on the mesas, a quiet boy with restless feet and a mind that wandered beyond the horizon.

One morning, he left. He told no one where he was going. He walked east, toward the rising sun, carrying nothing but a water gourd and a piece of dried corn.

He walked for many days. The mesas gave way to valleys, the valleys to plains, the plains to mountains he had never seen. He crossed rivers too wide to see the other side and climbed passes where the air was thin enough to make him dizzy.

Guided by Spider Grandmother — who appeared to him as an old woman sitting by a fire — he found his way to a body of water so vast it might have been the edge of the world. On the other side, he could see mountains glowing with a light that was not sunlight.

Spider Grandmother taught him to build a boat from reeds and to navigate by the stars. He crossed the water and found a land where spirits lived in houses of cloud and spoke in songs. They taught him sacred ceremonies — dances that brought rain, songs that healed the sick, prayers that opened the way between the living and the dead.

He stayed for one year, learning everything the spirits could teach. When he returned to his people, he brought new dances, new songs, and new knowledge of agriculture — how to read the stars to know when to plant, how to read the clouds to know when rain was coming.

The people benefited from his journey. The corn grew taller. The children grew stronger. The ceremonies became richer.

The boy — for he was still a boy, though his eyes were old — never spoke about where he had been. But sometimes, at night, he would sit outside his lodge and look east, toward the water he had crossed, and the people knew that the knowledge he carried had come from a place beyond the ordinary world.

title: The Boy Hunter Who Never Sacrificed to the Deer
summary: A Zuni story about a boy who was an excellent hunter but never performed the proper sacrifices or prayers to the spirits of the deer he killed. As a result, the deer spirits became angry. The boy's disrespectful hunting caused supernatural consequences — his kills became tainted, and he began to have bad luck. The spirits of the deer he had killed without proper ceremony confronted him. To make amends, the boy had to learn the proper rituals of the hunt, including making prayer sticks, offering cornmeal, and speaking words of gratitude to the deer's spirit. This story explains the origin of the Society of Rattlesnakes, which has the power to heal snakebites and conduct ceremonies that maintain balance between humans and animals. The story reinforces the Zuni teaching that all life is sacred and must be taken with gratitude and proper ceremony.
full_text:
He was an excellent hunter — the best in his village, perhaps the best in all Zuni country. His arrow never missed. His tracking was uncanny. He could read the signs of deer the way a priest reads the stars.

But he never performed the proper sacrifices. He never offered cornmeal to the spirits of the deer he killed. He never spoke words of gratitude over the body of the animal. He took without asking, killed without ceremony, and he wasted what he did not eat.

At first, nothing seemed wrong. The deer came easily, as they always had. But the spirits of the deer noticed. They gathered in the shadow world beneath the earth and spoke of the hunter's disrespect.

The consequences came slowly, then all at once. The hunter's luck soured. His arrows flew wide. His legs grew heavy on the chase. The deer he wounded escaped into the brush and died where he could not find them. His kills became tainted — the meat rotted overnight, the hides cracked and split.

Then the spirits of the deer he had killed without proper ceremony came to him in dreams. They stood around his sleeping body, their antlers crowned with starlight, their eyes holding the sorrow of beings who had given their lives without being honored.

"You took us without thanks," they said. "You ate us without prayer. You wore our skins without acknowledging our sacrifice. The balance is broken."

The hunter woke in terror. He went to the medicine people and told them what he had seen. They taught him the proper rituals — how to make prayer sticks from willow and feathers, how to scatter cornmeal at the four directions, how to speak words of gratitude to the deer's spirit before drawing the bow.

He performed every ceremony with sincerity. Gradually, his luck returned. The deer came again. The meat was sweet, the hides supple.

This story explains the origin of the Society of Rattlesnakes, which has the power to heal snakebites and conduct ceremonies that maintain balance between humans and animals. The story reinforces the Zuni teaching that all life is sacred and must be taken with gratitude and proper ceremony — for even the spirits of the dead demand justice.

title: The Blackfoot Creation: Apistotoke, Na'pi, and the World
summary: Apistotoke (Ihtsipatapiyohpa), the Great Spirit, created first the Sky Beings: Naato'si the Sun, Ko'komiki'somm the Moon, and the stars including Aapisowaahs the Morning Star. He then created Ksahkomitapi (Earth) as mother to all creation. Apistotoke created Na'pi (Old Man), the first man and demigod who shaped the world with his wife Kipitaakii (Old Lady). Using mud collected by Turtle during a great flood, Na'pi designed the earth, then created men, women, animals, and plants. He taught the Blackfoot people which plants to eat and animals to hunt, especially the buffalo.
full_text:
Apistotoke — called Ihtsipatapiyohpa, the Old Man Who Creates Us By Thought — stood in the void before creation. There was nothing around him. No ground beneath his feet, no sky above his head. Only the darkness and the silence and the power of his own mind.

He thought, and the thought became Sky Beings. Naato'si the Sun was the first — a being of fire and light who would illuminate everything that followed. Ko'komiki'somm the Moon was the second — a being of silver and shadow who would govern the night. And the stars came after, scattered across the sky like embers from a fire.

Then Apistotoke created Ksahkomitapi — the Earth — as mother to all creation. She was the ground beneath the sky, the body that held the roots, the foundation upon which all life would build.

Apistotoke then created Na'pi — Old Man — the first man and demigod who would shape the world with his own hands. Na'pi was not merely a human but a being of creative power, capable of molding the earth like clay and breathing life into the forms he made.

With his wife Kipitaakii — Old Lady — Na'pi set about the work of creation. They made the mountains and the valleys, the rivers and the lakes, the forests and the plains.

But the earth was covered in water. A great flood had washed over the land, and nothing grew. Na'pi sent Turtle to dive to the bottom of the flood and bring up mud. Turtle dove deep — deeper than any creature had gone before — and surfaced with a pawful of mud in his webbed hand.

Na'pi took the mud and shaped it. He molded it into hills and plains, into riverbeds and lake beds. He placed the mud on the back of a great turtle, and the mud grew, spreading across the shell until it became the land — Turtle Island, the Blackfoot call it.

Na'pi created men and women, animals and plants. He taught the Blackfoot people which plants to eat and which to avoid. He showed them which animals to hunt — especially the buffalo, whose body provided food, clothing, shelter, and tools.

When his work was done, Na'pi departed. He walked toward the western mountain and disappeared into the sunset. But his creation endures — the land, the people, the buffalo, the stars — all of it the thought of Apistotoke, shaped by the hands of Na'pi.

title: The Beaver Bundle Ceremony
summary: The Beaver Bundle is the most sacred medicine bundle of the Blackfoot people, said to have been given by the underwater spirits. According to legend, a Blackfoot man encountered beavers who taught him sacred songs, rituals, and the use of medicinal plants. The bundle contains various sacred objects including animal skins, pipes, and herbs, each with specific powers. The Beaver Bundle ceremony involves elaborate rituals, singing, and smoking the pipe. It is used for healing, ensuring good fortune, and maintaining the balance between the human and spirit worlds. The bundle is passed down through generations with great ceremony.
full_text:
A young man of the Lakota had been cursed by a medicine man who envied his success with the women of the village. The curse took the form of a persistent illness that no healer could cure — his skin turned gray, his eyes dimmed, and a heaviness settled over him like a blanket of stone.

The young man's grandmother, who remembered the old ways, told him to seek a vision. She prepared him for the quest — fasting, praying, smudging him with sage. He climbed to the top of the highest hill he could find and lay down beneath the stars.

For three days and three nights he fasted. On the fourth night, a figure appeared in his vision — a warrior dressed in the feathers of the eagle and the hide of the bear. The warrior spoke: "You have been cursed by human jealousy, but the spirits can break any curse. You must find the sacred root that grows where the lightning has struck and the rain has pooled. Brew it as tea and drink it at dawn."

The young man returned to his village and searched for the root. He found it growing in a meadow where a lightning bolt had split an oak tree and rain had gathered in the wound. He brewed the tea and drank it at dawn, and the curse lifted from him like smoke.

The story teaches that visions are not mere dreams but communications from the spirit world, and that the remedies for spiritual illness often come from unexpected sources.

title: Baaxpée and the Vision Quest
summary: Baaxpée is the sacred power of God (Akbaatatdia) in Crow belief, meaning 'power transcending the ordinary.' To acquire Baaxpée, a Crow must go on a vision quest (bilisshíissanne—'to fast from water'). The quester goes alone to an isolated peak, usually in the Wolf Mountains, fasting without food or water for two to three days. Self-mortification, including finger removal, is sometimes offered to show devotion. When a spirit pities the quester, it induces a vision, adopting the Crow as a child and bestowing Baaxpée. The spirit becomes a 'Medicine Father' who guides the Crow throughout life. The quester creates a Xapáaliia (medicine object) to represent the bond.
full_text:
A young Crow man fell in love with a woman from a rival tribe. Their love was forbidden, and the elders of both tribes opposed the match. But the lovers met secretly, exchanging gifts and whispered promises.

When their love was discovered, the young man was banished from his tribe. He traveled to the woman's village and was accepted there. Together they had children, and their descendants bridged the two tribes.

Over time, the marriage led to peace between the tribes. The story teaches that love can overcome the boundaries of tribe and tradition, and that the children of forbidden unions often bring healing to divided peoples.

title: The Birth of the Twin Brothers: Sapling and Flint
summary: After Sky Woman's daughter Tekawerahkwa (Breath of the Wind) gave birth, the twin boys emerged in different ways. The right-handed twin, Sapling (Hahgwehdi-yu or Kanehtó:ton), was born naturally and became the creator of all that is good and beautiful in the world. The left-handed twin, Flint (Hahgwehdaetgah or Okarahtsikó:wa), forced his way out through his mother's armpit, killing her. From her buried body grew the sacred plants: tobacco from her heart and strawberries from her feet. The twins then set about completing the creation, each making their own contributions to the natural world, with Flint attempting to undo all of Sapling's good work.
source: Kanehsatake Voices; native-languages.org Iroquois Creation Story; sacred-texts.com Onondaga version
full_text:
After Sky Woman's daughter Tekawerahkwa — Breath of the Wind — gave birth, the twin boys emerged in different ways, each one announcing his nature from the moment of birth.

The right-handed twin, Sapling — Hahgwehdi-yu or Kanehtó:ton — was born naturally. He came into the world gently, as if the earth itself had welcomed him. He was the creator of all that is good and beautiful — the flowers, the rivers, the gentle animals, the warm winds of spring.

The left-handed twin, Flint — Hahgwehdaetgah or Okarahtsikó:wa — forced his way out through his mother's armpit, killing her. His birth was violent, and his nature was sharp and cold. From his very first act, he brought death into the world.

From Tekawerahkwa's buried body grew the sacred plants. Tobacco sprang from her heart — the plant that carries prayers to the sky. Strawberries grew from her feet — the first fruit of the earth, sweet and red and round. The Three Sisters — corn, beans, and squash — grew from her body, each one a gift to the people.

The twins then set about completing the creation. Sapling made gentle animals — deer that would not harm humans, birds that would sing, fish that would swim in clear streams. Flint made dangerous creatures — wolves, bears, serpents — to balance the gentle ones.

Sapling made rivers flow downhill. Flint made them flow uphill. Sapling made fruit trees grow toward the sky. Flint made roots dig into the darkness. They were opposites, and they could not agree on anything.

But their opposition was necessary. Without Flint, there would be no challenge, no growth, no change. Without Sapling, there would be no beauty, no kindness, no hope. The world needed both — light and darkness, creation and destruction, life and death.

The story teaches the Haudenosaunee understanding that the world is shaped by opposing forces, and that balance is not the absence of conflict but the harmony of opposites.

title: The Battle of the Twins
summary: Sapling and Flint's conflict over the world they had created came to a head when they agreed to settle their rivalry through combat. Sapling chose the branches of the giant crab apple tree as his weapon, while Flint preferred poisonous roots, monster's teeth, and serpent fangs. They fought for many days across the landscape. The battle ended when Sapling overthrew Flint. He sent his evil brother to live in the underworld, but could not destroy him entirely. It was agreed that the world would need both good and evil, light and darkness. Even in victory, Sapling decreed that his brother would continue to influence the world, bringing winter, darkness, and death to balance the good he had created.
source: native-languages.org; Smith, Erminnie A. - Myths of the Iroquois (Project Gutenberg)
full_text:
Sapling and Flint's conflict over the world they had created came to a head when they agreed to settle their rivalry through combat. Each brother would choose his weapons and fight until one yielded.

Sapling chose the branches of the giant crab apple tree — flexible, green, alive with the power of growth. Flint chose poisonous roots, monster's teeth, and serpent fangs — weapons of decay and death.

They fought for many days across the landscape. Sapling's blows left fields of flowers in their wake. Flint's blows left dead trees and frozen ground. The battle raged from the eastern ocean to the western mountains, reshaping the land as they fought.

Where Sapling struck, hills rose and valleys formed. Where Flint struck, rivers cut through stone and canyons opened. The landscape of the Haudenosaunee world was being written in the violence of their combat.

Finally, Sapling overthrew Flint. He sent his evil brother to live in the underworld — the realm below the earth where darkness and cold prevail. But he could not destroy Flint entirely, for to destroy Flint would be to destroy half the world.

It was agreed that the world would need both good and evil, light and darkness. Even in victory, Sapling decreed that his brother would continue to influence the world. Flint would bring winter, darkness, and death to balance the good that Sapling had created.

The seasons reflect this eternal struggle. Spring and summer are Sapling's reign — warm, green, full of life. Autumn and winter are Flint's — cold, bare, full of death. But neither season lasts forever. Spring always returns, and winter always follows.

The story teaches that the cycle of seasons is not mere astronomy but the ongoing battle between two brothers whose love and hatred for each other shape the world.

title: The Big House Ceremony (Xinkwikaon)
summary: The Big House Ceremony is the paramount spiritual tradition of the Lenape people. According to oral tradition, the ceremony was given to the ancestors long ago when the people lived in the East. It is held in a special longhouse built to face the east, with carved faces on the center posts representing the Creator and the spirits. The ceremony lasts for twelve nights, during which the people pray, sing, and dance to fulfill their obligations to the spiritual forces of the universe. Participants use turtle-shell rattles and carved drumsticks, and each night a new fire is kindled with a fire-drill. The ceremony expresses gratitude to Kishelamakank, the four directions, and all of creation. The tradition declined during the forced removals but was revived through the dedication of elders who preserved the sacred songs and the original words.
source: Speck, Frank G. - A Study of the Delaware Indian Big House Ceremony; Harrington - Religion and Ceremonies of the Lenape
full_text:
The Big House Ceremony is the paramount spiritual tradition of the Lenape people. According to oral tradition, the ceremony was given to the ancestors long ago when the people lived in the East, in a land of green hills and clear rivers.

The ceremony is held in a special longhouse built to face the east, with carved faces on the center posts representing the Creator and the spirits. The longhouse is not merely a building but a living entity — its walls are the boundary between the ordinary world and the sacred, its fire is the heart of the ceremony.

The ceremony lasts for twelve nights. Each night, the people gather to pray, sing, and dance to fulfill their obligations to the spiritual forces of the universe. They use turtle-shell rattles and carved drumsticks, and each night a new fire is kindled with a fire-drill — a pointed stick spun against a flat piece of wood until smoke appears and flame ignites.

The ceremony expresses gratitude to Kishelamakank, the four directions, and all of creation. The songs are ancient — passed down from generation to generation, each word preserved exactly as it was first sung. The dances follow patterns that mirror the movements of the stars, the seasons, the cycles of life and death.

The tradition declined during the forced removals, when the Lenape were driven from their ancestral lands. Many ceremonies were lost. But through the dedication of elders who preserved the sacred songs and the original words, the Big House Ceremony was revived.

Today, the Lenape perform the ceremony in the traditional way, facing east, kindling the fire with a drill, singing the ancient songs. The ceremony is a thread that connects the present to the past, the living to the dead, the human to the divine.

title: The Big White Dog and the Sacred Pole (Chickasaw)
summary: In this Chickasaw origin story, a great white dog led the people on their migration and guided them with the sacred pole. The white dog was sent by Ababinili to protect the Chickasaw people during their long journey from the west. Each day, the dog would lead the way, and at night, the sacred pole was planted in the ground. The direction the pole leaned would indicate the path for the next day's travel. After many years, the pole finally stood upright at the site where the Chickasaw would settle. The great white dog then disappeared, its mission complete. The white dog is honored in Chickasaw tradition as a symbol of faithfulness, protection, and divine guidance. The story emphasizes the Chickasaw belief that animals are spiritual beings sent to assist humans.
full_text:
In this Chickasaw origin story, a great white dog led the people on their migration and guided them with the sacred pole. The white dog was sent by Ababinili to protect the Chickasaw people during their long journey from the west — a journey that lasted generations, that crossed rivers and mountains and deserts, and that tested the people's faith and endurance.

Each day, the dog would lead the way. It walked ahead of the people, its white coat bright against the dark earth, its ears alert, its nose reading the wind. It knew the path as if it had walked it a thousand times before — because, the elders said, it had. The white dog had been sent by Ababinili, and Ababinili had shown it the way.

At night, the sacred pole was planted in the ground. It was a white pole, made of dogwood, and it was smooth and straight as a column of light. When it was planted, it leaned — always, always — in the direction the people should travel next. The direction the pole leaned would indicate the path for the next day's travel.

After many years, the pole finally stood upright at the site where the Chickasaw would settle. It did not lean. It stood straight as an arrow, its tip pointing directly at the sky, as if it had found the place where the earth and heaven met. The people knew they had arrived.

The great white dog then disappeared, its mission complete. Some say it walked into the forest and was never seen again. Others say it lay down at the base of the sacred pole and turned to stone, becoming a guardian of the place where the people had found their home. Still others say it ascended to the sky, returning to Ababinili, its work well done.

The white dog is honored in Chickasaw tradition as a symbol of faithfulness, protection, and divine guidance. Dogs are treated with respect in Chickasaw communities, fed before humans eat, and given a place of honor in the home. The story emphasizes the Chickasaw belief that animals are spiritual beings sent to assist humans — that the relationship between humans and animals is not one of master and servant, but of partners in a shared journey.

title: The Bear Mother (Haida)
summary: In this classic Haida narrative, a woman who mocked the bears was taken by a bear who made her his wife. She was led into the bear's den deep in the forest, where she lived among the bear people and bore children who were half-human, half-bear. Her human brothers eventually tracked her down and killed the bears in a great hunt, but the woman herself had been transformed by her time with the bears. This story, common across many Northwest Coast tribes including the Tlingit version known as Kaats' and the Bear, serves to explain the special relationship between humans and bears. The bear woman's children became powerful ancestors, and her story validates the bear as a crest figure for certain clans. It also teaches respect for all animal people and warns against the dangers of disrespecting the natural world.
source: Haida oral tradition; Robert Bringhurst, A Story as Sharp as a Knife
full_text:
In this classic Haida narrative, a woman who mocked the bears was taken by a bear who made her his wife. She had been walking through the forest with her friends, and they had seen a bear — a great black bear, standing on its hind legs, its fur glistening with moisture. The woman laughed at the bear, pointing and calling it names, and her friends laughed with her.

The bear heard her. It dropped to all fours and followed them, silent as a shadow. When the woman separated from her friends, the bear appeared. It was enormous — taller than a man when it stood, its shoulders broad as a doorway, its claws as long as a man's finger. But it did not attack. It spoke.

The bear told the woman that she had insulted him, and that she must come with him to make amends. The woman was terrified, but she went. The bear led her deep into the forest, to a den beneath the roots of a great cedar. There, among the stone walls and the smell of earth, she lived with the bear people.

The bear people were not simply animals. They lived like humans inside their lodges — they cooked, they carved, they told stories — but to outsiders they appeared as bears. The woman learned their ways, and she bore children who were half-human, half-bear. These children were strong and strange, with their mother's face and their father's fur, with human hands and bear claws.

Her human brothers eventually tracked her down. They followed her trail — the broken branches, the scuffed earth, the scent of bear — and they found the den. They killed the bears in a great hunt, their spears flashing in the dim light of the forest. But the woman herself had been transformed by her time with the bears. She was no longer fully human; the forest had changed her, the bear people had remade her.

This story, common across many Northwest Coast tribes including the Tlingit version known as Kaats' and the Bear, serves to explain the special relationship between humans and bears. The bear woman's children became powerful ancestors, and her story validates the bear as a crest figure for certain clans. It also teaches respect for all animal people and warns against the dangers of disrespecting the natural world.

title: Bukwus the Wild Man of the Woods (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: Bukwus is the male counterpart of D'Sonoqua, the Wild Man of the Woods in Kwakwaka'wakw mythology. He is a hairy, giant being who lives in the deep forests and is associated with the spirits of those who died by starvation or exposure. Bukwus roams the woods calling out in a hollow voice, trying to lure humans into the forest with promises of food. He is particularly dangerous because he appears as a starving, pitiful figure who begs for help, but anyone who follows him becomes lost forever and joins his ghostly company. Unlike D'Sonoqua, who is more easily outwitted, Bukwus is treacherous and deceptive. However, like D'Sonoqua, he is also associated with great wealth and can bestow supernatural powers upon those who manage to survive an encounter with him. Bukwus appears in both the T'seka (Red Cedar Bark Ceremonies) and the Tła'sala (Peace Dances), where dancers wear masks depicting his gaunt, haunted features.
source: Franz Boas, Kwakiutl Ethnography; Kwakwaka'wakw oral tradition
full_text:
Bukwus is the male counterpart of D'Sonoqua, the Wild Man of the Woods in Kwakwaka'wakw mythology. He is a hairy, giant being who lives in the deep forests, in the places where the trees grow so thick that the sky is invisible and the ground is carpeted with moss so deep that a person can sink to their knees.

Bukwus is associated with the spirits of those who died by starvation or exposure — the unfortunates who perished in the wilderness, whose bodies were never found, whose names were never spoken. Their spirits lingered in the forest, and Bukwus was their keeper, their warden, their king.

He roams the woods calling out in a hollow voice, trying to lure humans into the forest with promises of food. The voice is thin and reedy, like the sound of wind through dead branches, and it carries a melody that is almost beautiful but ultimately wrong — a melody that promises warmth but delivers cold, that promises fullness but delivers emptiness.

He is particularly dangerous because he appears as a starving, pitiful figure who begs for help. He stands at the edge of the trail, his body gaunt, his eyes hollow, his arms extended in a gesture of need. Anyone who follows him becomes lost forever and joins his ghostly company.

Unlike D'Sonoqua, who is more easily outwitted, Bukwus is treacherous and deceptive. He does not simply grab his victims — he lures them, guides them, leads them deeper and deeper into the forest until they cannot find their way out. The trail disappears. The landmarks change. The trees look the same in every direction. And Bukwus walks ahead, his hollow voice calling, his gaunt figure visible for just a moment before it vanishes into the shadows.

However, like D'Sonoqua, he is also associated with great wealth and can bestow supernatural powers upon those who manage to survive an encounter with him. A person who escapes Bukwus gains knowledge of the forest that no other human possesses — the location of hidden springs, the trails of supernatural beings, the songs that open the doors between worlds.

Bukwus appears in both the T'seka — Red Cedar Bark Ceremonies — and the Tla'sala — Peace Dances — where dancers wear masks depicting his gaunt, haunted features.

title: Blue Jay Visits Ghost Town (Chinook - Ioi and Blue Jay)
summary: Blue Jay's sister Ioi was bought by ghosts as a wife and disappeared to the land of the dead. After a year, Blue Jay went searching for her. He asked all the trees and birds where people go when they die. He journeyed to the ghost town, which appeared to him as a place of bones and decay, but the ghosts saw it as beautiful. Ioi warned Blue Jay not to laugh at the ghosts or behave disrespectfully, but Blue Jay could not control himself. He kicked skulls, laughed at the skeletons, and shouted at the ghost people who were only skeletons to his eyes. When the ghosts went to butcher a whale, Blue Jay saw only a beached skeleton. When they brought in firewood, he saw only bark. Ioi kept explaining that his eyes saw differently because he was alive — the ghosts saw everything as beautiful. He tried to join the ghost dances, but when the ghosts danced gracefully, Blue Jay stood on his head. He died a second time and remained in the ghost world forever. This haunting story explores the boundary between life and death and the dangers of lacking respect for the supernatural world.
source: Chinook Texts, Smithsonian Institution; Chinook oral tradition from Charles Cultee
full_text:
Blue Jay's sister Ioi was gone. She had been bought by ghosts as a wife — purchased with ghost-money, traded like property, taken to the land of the dead. The ghosts had come to the village one night, silent and pale, and they had selected Ioi from among the women, and she had disappeared with them, and the living world was poorer for her absence.

Blue Jay mourned. He mourned loudly, as he did everything, with tears and wailing and dramatic pronouncements of grief. But mourning was not enough. He wanted his sister back.

After a year, Blue Jay went searching for her. He asked everyone he met — the trees, the birds, the animals, the rivers — where people go when they die. The trees told him nothing. The birds told him nothing. The rivers, flowing endlessly toward the sea, told him nothing.

Finally, a salmon — old, wise, its scales worn smooth by years of swimming — told him: "The dead live in a town at the end of the world. Go west, past the last mountain, past the last river, and you will find it."

Blue Jay went west. He walked for days, past mountains that scraped the sky, past rivers that ran black with depth, past forests so old that the trees had forgotten they were trees. And at the end of the world, he found the ghost town.

To Blue Jay's living eyes, the ghost town was a place of bones and decay. The houses were made of ribs and vertebrae, lashed together with sinew. The ground was covered in ash. The sky was the color of old bruises. Everything was broken, hollow, dead.

But Ioi was there. She stood at the entrance to the town, waiting for him, and she was not dead — not entirely. She was translucent, like smoke, and her voice was thin, but she was his sister, and she was glad to see him.

"Do not laugh," she warned him. "Do not behave disrespectfully. The ghosts have their own ways, and you must honor them."

Blue Jay promised. He promised sincerely, with all the sincerity of a being who could not keep a promise if his life depended on it.

He entered the ghost town, and the ghosts welcomed him. They gave him food — or what they called food. To Blue Jay's living eyes, it was rot and decay, maggots and mold. But the ghosts ate it with relish, and their eyes were bright, and they seemed content.

When the ghosts went to butcher a whale that had washed ashore, Blue Jay saw only a beached skeleton. When they brought in firewood, he saw only bark and splinters. When they danced, he saw only bones clicking together in the dim light.

"You see things differently because you are alive," Ioi explained. "To us, everything is beautiful."

Blue Jay could not help himself. He kicked the skulls that lay in the street. He laughed at the skeletons who tried to serve him food. He shouted at the ghost children who had no flesh on their faces.

And when the ghosts danced — gracefully, beautifully, in patterns that represented the seasons and the stars and the turning of the world — Blue Jay stood on his head.

The ghosts were offended. The spirits of the dead do not tolerate disrespect, and Blue Jay had been disrespectful in every way a living being can be. He died a second time and remained in the ghost world forever.

This haunting story explores the boundary between life and death and the dangers of lacking respect for the supernatural world. The living and the dead perceive reality differently, and the gap between their perceptions cannot be bridged by laughter or contempt. Blue Jay, who could not see the beauty of the ghost world, was destroyed by his own blindness.

title: Blue Jay Finds a Wife (Chinook)
summary: Ioi decided it was high time for Blue Jay to quit his playful trickery and settle down with a wife. She told him he must select a wife from the land of the dead, from the Supernatural People. Ioi recommended that Blue Jay choose an old woman and suggested the recently deceased wife of a chief. Blue Jay went to the ghost town and courted the ghost woman. True to his nature, he behaved foolishly, misinterpreting the customs of the dead and acting disrespectfully. He made inappropriate jokes and did not understand that the ghosts perceived reality differently than the living. Despite Ioi's warnings, Blue Jay's behavior caused chaos in the ghost village. The story highlights Blue Jay's inability to mature and learn from experience, making him a comic but ultimately tragic figure. It is also one of several Chinook stories that explore the relationship between the living and the dead, suggesting that the boundary between worlds must be approached with humility and respect.
full_text:
Ioi had been patient with her brother for a long time. Too long. Blue Jay was a fool — everyone knew it, including Blue Jay, though he would never admit it — and fools need wives to keep them from getting into trouble. At least, that was Ioi's theory.

"It is high time you settled down," she told him. "You cannot wander the world forever, getting into fights, bragging about things you have not done, and offending everyone you meet."

Blue Jay ruffled his feathers. "I am perfectly capable of taking care of myself."

"You got into a fight with a tree last week," Ioi said.

"The tree started it."

"You set fire to a river."

"It was a small fire."

Ioi sighed. "You must select a wife."

Blue Jay was interested. He had never thought much about wives — they seemed like a lot of work — but the idea of having someone to cook for him and tell him how wonderful he was had a certain appeal.

"Where will I find a wife?" he asked.

Ioi told him: he must go to the land of the dead, to the ghost town at the end of the world, and choose a wife from among the Supernatural People. The ghosts had beautiful women, she said, and they would be willing to trade.

She recommended that Blue Jay choose an old woman — someone experienced, someone who would not be impressed by his nonsense, someone who could keep him in line. Specifically, she suggested the recently deceased wife of a chief, who was said to be wise and patient.

Blue Jay went to the ghost town. He found the old woman, and he began to court her, in his fashion — which is to say, he behaved foolishly, misinterpreted every custom he encountered, and acted with the kind of disrespectful enthusiasm that made the ghosts wish they had stayed dead.

He did not understand that the ghosts perceived reality differently than the living. Where he saw bones, they saw beautiful furniture. Where he saw rot, they saw fine food. Where he saw ash, they saw soft earth. He commented loudly on the ugliness of everything, and the ghosts, who were proud of their town, were offended.

He made jokes about death, which the ghosts did not find funny because death was not an abstraction to them — it was their daily reality. He mocked their ceremonies, which were sacred and ancient and not subject to ridicule. He ate their food and pronounced it terrible, not knowing that to the ghosts it was a feast fit for spirits.

Ioi's warnings echoed in his mind, but Blue Jay could not heed them. He was constitutionally incapable of behaving with decorum, and the ghost town was the one place in the universe where decorum was not optional.

The ghosts drove him out. They chased him with sticks and stones and the fury of beings who had been deeply, personally insulted. Blue Jay fled, squawking and flapping, and he never returned.

The story highlights Blue Jay's inability to mature and learn from experience, making him a comic but ultimately tragic figure. It is also one of several Chinook stories that explore the relationship between the living and the dead, suggesting that the boundary between worlds must be approached with humility and respect — two qualities that Blue Jay possessed in smaller quantities than any being in the Chinook world.

title: The Bluejay Cycle (Coast Salish)
summary: Bluejay is a prominent trickster figure in Coast Salish mythology, particularly among the Chemainus, Cowichan, and other Salish communities. He is generally a benevolent being who helps people, but he is also extremely foolish and careless, and stories about him are often humorous or slapstick. In one classic story, Bluejay boasted that he could steal the sun, but his lies got him into trouble when the people took him seriously and he had to deliver on his impossible promise. In another, he tried to imitate the skills of other animals and birds, with disastrously funny results. Bluejay often interacts with his long-suffering sister Ioi, who tries to keep him out of trouble but fails because Bluejay refuses to listen to good advice. Unlike Raven, who possesses genuine supernatural power, Bluejay's adventures typically stem from his foolishness rather than malice. The Bluejay stories serve as comic relief in the storytelling tradition while also teaching lessons about humility, honesty, and the dangers of boastfulness.
source: Coast Salish oral tradition; Salish Myths and Legends (University of Nebraska Press)
full_text:
Bluejay is a prominent trickster figure in Coast Salish mythology, particularly among the Chemainus, Cowichan, and other Salish communities along the Strait of Georgia and the Fraser River. He is not like Raven — not powerful, not wise, not possessed of genuine supernatural gifts. Bluejay is, above all, foolish. And it is his foolishness, not his cleverness, that drives his stories.

In one classic tale, Bluejay boasted that he could steal the sun. He announced this at a feast, standing on a cedar plank and squawking his declaration to the assembled people. Everyone laughed, but Bluejay took their laughter as encouragement. He flew up into the sky, flapping his blue wings, squawking louder and louder, getting closer and closer to the sun.

The sun, unimpressed, simply grew hotter. Bluejay's feathers began to smolder. His beak started to melt. He squawked in panic and tumbled back to earth, landing in a creek where the water sizzled and steamed around him. He emerged singed, humiliated, and hungry — which was, in many ways, his natural state.

In another story, Bluejay tried to imitate the skills of other animals and birds. He watched Eagle catch a salmon and tried to do the same, but he could not dive fast enough and hit the water face-first. He watched Owl hunt mice and tried to do the same, but his eyes were too bright and the mice saw him coming. He watched Bear catch berries and tried to do the same, but he fell out of the berry bush and landed in a thorn patch.

Bluejay often interacts with his long-suffering sister Ioi, who tries to keep him out of trouble. Ioi is the voice of reason, the voice of caution, the voice of "please stop talking and think about what you are doing for once in your life." But Bluejay refuses to listen to good advice, and his adventures inevitably end in disaster — for himself, and often for anyone unlucky enough to be nearby.

Unlike Raven, who possesses genuine supernatural power and uses it to reshape the world, Bluejay's adventures typically stem from his foolishness rather than malice. He does not set out to harm anyone; he simply cannot help being himself. He is loud where he should be quiet, brave where he should be cautious, and certain where he should be doubtful.

The Bluejay stories serve as comic relief in the storytelling tradition while also teaching lessons about humility, honesty, and the dangers of boastfulness. Every community has its Bluejays — the ones who talk too much, who promise too much, who believe their own press releases — and the stories about Bluejay remind listeners that the gap between what you say you can do and what you can actually do is a dangerous place to live.

title: The Bear Who Married a Woman (Tsimshian)
summary: A Tsimshian woman gathering berries in the forest encountered a bear who removed his bearskin and revealed himself as a handsome man. He took her to his village, where the bear people lived just like humans inside their lodges but appeared as bears to outsiders. The woman married him, learned the ways of the bear people, and gave birth to children who were half-human, half-bear. Her husband provided abundantly for her, bringing salmon and berries. She grew content with her bear husband, but when her human brothers came searching for her, she was forced to choose between her two families. The brothers killed the bear husband in a hunt, but the woman begged them not to harm her children. The children grew up with special powers of communication between humans and bears. Their descendants became the Bear Clan. This cross-cultural marriage story, found throughout the Northwest Coast, establishes the bear as a relative rather than an animal, requiring respect and proper protocol in hunting.
source: Tsimshian oral tradition; Franz Boas, Tsimshian Mythology; native-languages.org
full_text:
A Tsimshian woman gathering berries in the forest encountered a bear who removed his bearskin and revealed himself as a handsome man. He stood before her in the forest clearing, his human body pale and strong, his eyes dark with an intelligence that was more than animal.

He took her to his village, where the bear people lived just like humans inside their lodges but appeared as bears to outsiders. The village was hidden in the deep forest, invisible to those who did not know where to look. Inside the lodges, the bear people cooked, carved, and told stories. Outside, they were bears — large, powerful, and solitary.

The woman married him, learned the ways of the bear people, and gave birth to children who were half-human, half-bear. Her husband provided abundantly for her, bringing salmon and berries, his bear strength making the hunt easy.

She grew content with her bear husband, but when her human brothers came searching for her, she was forced to choose between her two families. The brothers killed the bear husband in a hunt, their spears flashing in the dim light of the forest. But the woman begged them not to harm her children.

The children grew up with special powers of communication between humans and bears. They could speak both languages, understand both worlds, and move between them with ease. Their descendants became the Bear Clan.

This cross-cultural marriage story, found throughout the Northwest Coast, establishes the bear as a relative rather than an animal, requiring respect and proper protocol in hunting. To hunt a bear is not simply to take game; it is to take a relative, and the proper ceremonies must be observed.

title: Brer Rabbit and the Briar Patch (Bred and Bawn)
summary: After Brer Fox captures Brer Rabbit using the Tar-Baby, he declares his intent to kill and eat him. Brer Rabbit pleads for his life, begging not to be thrown into the briar patch, suggesting instead that he be roasted, hanged, drowned, or skinned. The more Brer Rabbit begs to avoid the briar patch, the more determined Brer Fox becomes to throw him there. Finally, Brer Fox snatches Brer Rabbit by the hind legs and flings him deep into the briar patch. To Brer Fox's astonishment, Brer Rabbit appears on a hillside, picking burrs from his fur, and shouts back: 'Bred en bawn in a brier-patch, Brer Fox—bred en bawn in a brier-patch!' The briar patch, which would tear the skin of any other creature, was Brer Rabbit's ancestral home.
source: Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings (Joel Chandler Harris, 1881)
full_text:
After Brer Fox captured Brer Rabbit using the Tar-Baby, he declared his intent to kill and eat him. This was not idle talk — Brer Fox had been planning this moment for weeks, and he had brought a rope.

But Brer Rabbit was not ready to die. He was never ready to die. He began to plead — not for his life, exactly, but for the manner of his death, because Brer Rabbit understood that the right words at the right time could change anything.

"Roast me over a slow fire," he said. "That's the worst thing you can do to me. I can't stand a slow fire."

Brer Fox considered this. A slow fire did sound like a lot of work. He'd have to gather wood, build a fire, watch it burn down to coals, and then tend it while Brer Rabbit roasted. That would take all afternoon.

"How about I drown you?" Brer Fox offered.

"Please, Brer Fox, not drowning!" Brer Rabbit cried. "I have a fear of water. I'd rather be hanged."

"Hanged?" Brer Fox considered this. Hanging required a tree with a sturdy branch, a rope, and time. It was simpler than a slow fire, but still involved effort.

"I tell you what," Brer Fox said. "I'll throw you in the briar patch."

Brer Rabbit's eyes went wide. "Not the briar patch!" he begged. "Please, Brer Fox, anything but the briar patch! Those thorns will tear me to pieces! I'll be skinned alive! Just kill me quick — roast me, drown me, hang me — but don't throw me in the briar patch!"

The more Brer Rabbit begged to avoid the briar patch, the more determined Brer Fox became to throw him there. It was, after all, the cruelest fate Brer Rabbit could imagine. Brer Fox wanted him to suffer.

Brer Fox snatched Brer Rabbit by the hind legs and flung him deep into the briar patch. The thorns caught at Brer Rabbit's fur, tore at his skin, scratched and ripped and tore.

Then Brer Fox heard a sound — a voice, coming from the hillside above. He looked up and saw Brer Rabbit sitting on a rock, picking burrs from his fur, grinning.

"Bred en bawn in a brier-patch, Brer Fox!" Brer Rabbit called out, laughing. "Bred en bawn in a brier-patch!" The briar patch, which would tear the skin of any other creature, was Brer Rabbit's ancestral home. He had been born there, raised there, and learned to navigate its thorns before he could walk. Brer Fox had played right into his hands.

title: Brer Rabbit's Laughing Place
summary: Brer Fox catches Brer Rabbit and declares he will finally kill him. Brer Rabbit, always quick-witted, says he does not care about dying but begs to be allowed to visit his 'laughing place' one last time to die happy. Curious, Brer Fox agrees and follows Brer Rabbit into the woods. Brer Rabbit leads him to a hollow tree filled with a swarm of angry bees. Brer Rabbit points to the tree and whispers that his laughing place is inside. When Brer Fox peers into the hollow, the bees swarm out and attack him furiously. While Brer Fox flees in agony, Brer Rabbit laughs himself silly and escapes once again, proving that his most dangerous weapon is his clever tongue.
source: African American oral tradition, collected in Uncle Remus stories
full_text:
Brer Fox caught Brer Rabbit again — the third time that month, which was either a testament to Brer Fox's persistence or a testament to Brer Rabbit's carelessness, depending on who was telling the story. This time, Brer Fox had a knife, and he was not interested in negotiation.

"I'm going to kill you, Brer Rabbit," he said, and his voice was flat and serious, without the theatrical menace of their usual encounters. This was real.

Brer Rabbit looked at the knife. He looked at Brer Fox. He calculated the distance to the nearest cover and determined it was too far. He was, for once, genuinely trapped.

"I don't care about dying," Brer Rabbit said, and his voice was quiet, almost resigned. "I've lived a good life. But I have one request."

Brer Fox paused. He was not a cruel being — not really — and the idea of granting a last request appealed to his sense of fairness.

"What is it?" he asked.

"I want to visit my laughing place one last time," Brer Rabbit said. "It's where I go when I want to be happy. If I can see it one more time, I'll die content."

Brer Fox was suspicious. Brer Rabbit was always suspicious. But the request seemed harmless enough — a small detour, a brief stop, and then Brer Fox could get on with his dinner.

"All right," he said. "Show me."

Brer Rabbit led Brer Fox into the woods, through a thicket of huckleberry bushes, past a stand of tall pines, to a hollow tree at the edge of a clearing. The tree was old, its trunk split by lightning, its interior a dark cavity that hummed with a strange sound.

"My laughing place is inside," Brer Rabbit whispered. "Listen."

Brer Fox leaned close to the hollow and listened. He heard a buzzing — a deep, resonant hum that grew louder the closer he put his ear. Curious, he peered into the darkness.

Inside the hollow tree was a swarm of angry bees.

They poured out of the darkness in a yellow-black cloud, their wings a blur, their stingers aimed at the nearest flesh. Brer Fox screamed and ran, flailing his arms, slapping at the bees that stung his ears, his nose, his eyes. He ran through the thicket, through the huckleberry bushes, through the creek, and he did not stop running until he was half a mile away, swollen and bleeding and bewildered.

Behind him, Brer Rabbit laughed himself silly.

title: Brer Rabbit and the Moon in the Millpond
summary: A classic African American trickster tale in which Brer Rabbit, feeling thirsty, goes to the millpond to drink and sees the moon reflected in the water. Mistaking it for a golden cheese wheel, he tries to retrieve it. Unable to reach it from the bank, he tricks Brer Fox into helping him by claiming there is a valuable treasure in the pond. Brer Fox ties a rope around Brer Rabbit's waist and lowers him down, but Brer Rabbit only stirs up the water, making the reflection disappear. He claims the treasure sank and convinces Brer Fox to jump in after it, leaving Brer Fox cold and humiliated while Brer Rabbit laughs and feasts on the cheese he finds elsewhere.
source: African American oral tradition (variant collected throughout the US South)
full_text:
A classic African American trickster tale in which Brer Rabbit, feeling thirsty, goes to the millpond to drink and sees the moon reflected in the water. The reflection was perfect — a full, golden disk floating on the surface, so bright and round that Brer Rabbit was certain it was a cheese wheel that had fallen from someone's pocket.

He reached for it. His paw broke the surface, and the cheese shattered into a thousand shimmering pieces. He waited for the water to still, and the cheese reformed — round and golden and just out of reach.

Brer Rabbit tried everything. He lay on his belly and stretched his arm as far as it would go. He climbed a tree and leaned down from a branch. He found a stick and poked at the water. Nothing worked. The cheese remained just beyond his grasp.

Then Brer Rabbit had an idea — the kind of idea that Brer Rabbit specialized in, the kind that involved someone else doing the hard work.

He went to Brer Fox. "Brer Fox," he said, "there is a treasure in the millpond. A golden treasure, so heavy it would take two of us to pull it out."

Brer Fox was interested. Brer Fox was always interested in treasure.

They went to the millpond together. Brer Rabbit tied a rope around his waist and had Brer Fox lower him into the water. As he descended, he splashed and thrashed, stirring up the mud at the bottom, turning the water brown and murky.

"I can see it!" Brer Rabbit shouted from beneath the surface. "It's beautiful! But it's slipping away!" He splashed harder, and the moon's reflection vanished entirely.

"It sank!" Brer Rabbit cried, emerging from the water covered in mud. "The treasure sank to the bottom! You have to jump in after it, Brer Fox!"

Brer Fox jumped in. He searched the murky water for the golden treasure, found nothing but mud and weeds, and emerged cold, humiliated, and empty-handed.

Brer Rabbit was already gone. He had found some cheese elsewhere — real cheese, from someone's cooling shelf — and was eating it on a stump, licking his paws and smiling at the moon.

title: Brer Rabbit Nibbles Up the Butter
summary: Brer Rabbit, Brer Fox, Brer Possum, and Brer Coon together churn butter and set it aside to share later. Brer Rabbit grows hungry and secretly eats all the butter. When the friends discover the butter is gone, Brer Rabbit blames Brer Possum and suggests they test who is guilty by having each lie down in the sun and see whose belly the butter melts from. Brer Rabbit arranges things so that Brer Possum ends up sitting on the butter smear, and when the sun warms him, the butter appears on his fur. Brer Possum is punished for Brer Rabbit's crime, while Brer Rabbit escapes blame through clever manipulation. The story explains why the possum plays dead when caught—he learned to be wary of being tricked again.
source: Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings (Joel Chandler Harris, 1881)
full_text:
Brer Rabbit, Brer Fox, Brer Possum, and Brer Coon gathered at Brer Fox's house on a Saturday morning and decided to churn butter. They poured cream into the churn, took turns at the dash, and worked until their arms ached and the butter came — a solid, golden lump that they scooped out and placed in a bowl.

"We'll set it aside and share it later," Brer Fox said, and they all agreed, because they were friends, and friends share butter.

But Brer Rabbit was hungry. Not the ordinary kind of hungry — the kind that sits in your stomach and whispers suggestions. He waited until the others were gone, then he crept back to Brer Fox's house and ate all the butter. Every bit of it. He licked the bowl clean, wiped it on his fur, and left.

When the friends gathered again to share the butter, they found the bowl empty.

"Who ate the butter?" Brer Fox demanded.

They looked at each other. Brer Possum looked guilty — he always looked guilty, because he was a nervous creature who sweated when he was accused of anything, even when he was innocent.

Brer Rabbit pointed at Brer Possum. "It must have been him," he said. "Look at him. He's sweating."

Brer Possum was indeed sweating, but not because he had eaten the butter. He was sweating because he was terrified of being accused.

"I didn't eat it!" Brer Possum wailed.

"We'll see about that," Brer Rabbit said. "Here's what we'll do. We'll all lie down in the sun, and whoever ate the butter, the butter will melt out of them and we'll see the proof."

The others agreed. They lay down in the sun, side by side. But before they lay down, Brer Rabbit secretly smeared the butter on the spot where Brer Possum would lie.

As the sun warmed Brer Possum, the butter melted and appeared on his fur, glistening in the light.

"See!" Brer Rabbit cried. "The butter is coming out of him!"

Brer Possum was punished for Brer Rabbit's crime, while Brer Rabbit escaped blame through clever manipulation. The story explains why the possum plays dead when caught — he learned to be wary of being tricked again.

title: Brer Rabbit Rides Brer Fox
summary: Brer Rabbit, seeking to prove his superiority, convinces Miss Meadows and the girls that he can ride Brer Fox like a horse. Brer Fox overhears this boast and vows revenge. The next day, Brer Rabbit pretends to be sick and asks Brer Fox to carry him to Miss Meadows's house. Once on Brer Fox's back, Brer Rabbit digs in his heels and rides Brer Fox straight to the gathering, where he shows off by declaring: 'This is the way I ride Brer Fox!' Humiliated, Brer Fox shakes him off, but Brer Rabbit escapes into a hollow tree. Brer Fox enlists Brer Wolf to help dig him out, but Brer Rabbit tricks them by claiming enemies are approaching and sends them fleeing. The tale is part of a cycle of African trickster stories also found in the Caribbean and South America.
source: Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings (Joel Chandler Harris, 1881)
full_text:
Brer Rabbit, seeking to prove his superiority over Brer Fox, convinced Miss Meadows and the girls that he could ride Brer Fox like a horse. This was, by any reasonable measure, an absurd claim. Brer Fox was a predator, and Brer Rabbit was prey, and the relationship between them did not include riding.

But Brer Rabbit was persuasive. He spoke with the confidence of someone who had never let the truth stand in the way of a good story, and Miss Meadows and the girls were charmed by his audacity.

Brer Fox overheard this boast and vowed revenge. The next day, Brer Rabbit pretended to be sick and asked Brer Fox to carry him to Miss Meadows's house. "I'm too weak to walk," he moaned. "If you carry me there, I'll owe you a favor."

Brer Fox agreed, thinking he would have his revenge when they arrived. But once on Brer Fox's back, Brer Rabbit dug in his heels and rode straight to the gathering, where he showed off by declaring: "This is the way I ride Brer Fox!"

Humiliated, Brer Fox shook him off, but Brer Rabbit escaped into a hollow tree. Brer Fox enlisted Brer Wolf to help dig him out, but Brer Rabbit tricked them by claiming enemies were approaching and sent them fleeing.

The tale is part of a cycle of African trickster stories also found in the Caribbean and South America, where the rabbit trickster rides the fox or the jaguar, demonstrating that wit can conquer power.

title: Brer Terrapin Outruns Brer Rabbit
summary: Brer Rabbit, proud of his speed, mocks Brer Terrapin for his slow, plodding pace. Brer Terrapin challenges Brer Rabbit to a race. Knowing he cannot win on speed alone, Brer Terrapin stations his wife and several family members at intervals along the race course. At each mile marker, Brer Rabbit calls out 'Brer Terrapin!' and one of the terrapin family calls back, 'Here I am!' After several such exchanges, Brer Rabbit grows exhausted and confused, unable to understand how the slow terrapin keeps ahead of him. When Brer Terrapin crosses the finish line first, Brer Rabbit collapses from exhaustion. The story—a variant of the tortoise and hare theme—is a cornerstone of African American animal folklore, reinforcing that patience and strategy triumph over arrogance.
source: African American oral tradition (Gullah Geechee and Uncle Remus variants)
full_text:
Brer Rabbit, proud of his speed, mocked Brer Terrapin for his slow, plodding pace. "You move like a rock rolling uphill," Brer Rabbit said. "If you were any slower, you'd be standing still."

Brer Terrapin was patient. He had been mocked before, and he had won before, and he knew that the race was not always to the swift.

"I challenge you to a race," Brer Terrapin said. "Ten miles. Winner takes the prize."

Brer Rabbit laughed. A race against a terrapin? This would be the easiest victory of his life.

But Brer Terrapin was clever. He station his wife and several family members at intervals along the race course — one at each mile marker. The plan was simple: Brer Rabbit would run ahead, reach a mile marker, and hear a voice calling out.

The race began. Brer Rabbit shot off the line like an arrow, leaving Brer Terrapin far behind. At the first mile marker, he called out: "Brer Terrapin!"

"Here I am!" a voice answered from the broomgrass.

Brer Rabbit ran faster. At the second mile marker: "Brer Terrapin!"

"Here I am!"

At the third, the fourth, the fifth — Brer Terrapin was always just ahead, always just out of reach. Brer Rabbit ran until his legs trembled and his lungs burned, but he could not shake the terrapin.

By the ninth mile, Brer Rabbit was exhausted. He stumbled, he panted, he questioned his sanity. How could a terrapin be ahead of him? He was the fastest creature in the forest!

At the finish line, Brer Terrapin was already there, sitting on a rock, waiting.

Brer Rabbit collapsed from exhaustion. The terrapin had won, and Brer Rabbit learned a lesson that speed alone does not win — strategy, family, and preparation are just as important as raw ability.

title: Brer Rabbit Finds His Match at Last
summary: Brer Rabbit, overconfident after countless successful tricks, encounters a creature he cannot outsmart. In some versions, it is Old Man Tarrypin (the terrapin) who turns the tables on Brer Rabbit; snip in others, it is a wise old woman or a young girl who matches wits with him. Brer Rabbit tries every trick in his repertoire—false friendliness, reverse psychology, flattery, and fear—but nothing works. The creature remains calm, sees through every deception, and ultimately traps Brer Rabbit in a situation where his cleverness fails him. Brer Rabbit must humble himself, admit defeat, and negotiate his release. This tale serves as a caution that even the most cunning trickster may eventually meet his match, reminding listeners that overconfidence is the trickster's own greatest vulnerability.
source: Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings (Joel Chandler Harris, 1881)
full_text:
Brer Rabbit, overconfident after countless successful tricks, encountered a creature he could not outsmart. It happened like this:

Brer Rabbit was walking through the forest when he met Old Man Tarrypin — the terrapin — sitting on a log, sunning himself. Brer Rabbit, feeling particularly clever that day, decided to play a trick on the old creature.

"Good morning, Old Man Tarrypin," he said. "Nice weather we're having."

"It is," the terrapin agreed.

"I suppose you're too slow to go anywhere in this nice weather," Brer Rabbit said.

"I go where I need to go," the terrapin said.

Brer Rabbit tried every trick in his repertoire. He tried false friendliness: "I'll carry you on my back, Old Man. You'll see the world." The terrapin declined. He tried reverse psychology: "I bet you're too scared to race me." The terrapin was not scared. He tried flattery: "Your shell is the most beautiful shell I've ever seen." The terrapin said thank you and went back to sunning himself.

Brer Rabbit tried fear: "There's a hawk overhead!" The terrapin pulled into his shell and waited. The hawk, if there was one, passed by.

Nothing worked. The terrapin remained calm, saw through every deception, and sat on his log like a rock — immovable, unshakable, unimpressed.

Finally, Brer Rabbit sat down beside the terrapin and admitted defeat. "I can't trick you," he said.

"No," the terrapin agreed. "You can't."

This tale serves as a caution that even the most cunning trickster may eventually meet his match, reminding listeners that overconfidence is the trickster's own greatest vulnerability.

title: The Boo Hag
summary: In Gullah Geechee folklore, a young man named Emmet Fisher falls in love with a beautiful but mysterious woman who lives deep in the marsh. Against all warnings, he marries her. One night, Emmet pretends to be asleep and witnesses his bride remove her skin, hang it on a hook, and transform into a skinless red creature with bat-like wings. She flies out through the keyhole to ride her victims—sitting on their chests and stealing their breath while they sleep. Emmet confronts her the next morning, but she denies everything. He sprinkles cayenne pepper and salt around the room, and when she sheds her skin again that night, she cannot put it back on—the pepper burns her raw flesh. She flees into the night, forever skinless. The Boo Hag legend explains why Gullah people paint their doors and windows 'haint blue,' hang brooms by the entrance, and keep salt and pepper mixtures in corners: all ways to confuse, repel, or trap these night-visiting entities that drain the life force of the living.
source: Gullah Geechee oral tradition; snip Federal Writers' Project Slave Narratives; snip Drums and Shadows (1940)
full_text:
In Gullah Geechee folklore, a young man named Emmet Fisher fell in love with a beautiful but mysterious woman who lived deep in the marsh. She appeared one evening at the edge of the water, her hair black as the night, her eyes dark and deep, her voice like honey over gravel. She said her name was nothing that he could pronounce, and she smiled in a way that made him forget his own.

Against all warnings — his grandmother told him not to go near the marsh, his mother told him to find a girl from the village, his friends told him there was something wrong about a woman who lived alone in the swamp — Emmet married her.

They lived together in his house, and for a time, everything was fine. She cooked for him, cleaned for him, lay beside him at night. But there was something wrong. She never ate in front of him. She never undressed in his presence. She left every night after he fell asleep and returned before dawn, smelling of marsh water and something else — something metallic, like blood.

One night, Emmet pretended to be asleep. He lay still, his eyes barely open, and watched his bride remove her skin. She peeled it off like a garment — first the arms, then the torso, then the legs — and hung it on a hook behind the door. Beneath the skin was a creature that was not human: a skinless red thing with bat-like wings and fingers that ended in claws.

She flew out through the keyhole to ride her victims — sitting on their chests and stealing their breath while they slept.

Emmet confronted her the next morning, but she denied everything. He sprinkled cayenne pepper and salt around the room, and when she shed her skin again that night, she could not put it back on — the pepper burned her raw flesh. She fled into the night, forever skinless.

The Boo Hag legend explains why Gullah people paint their doors and windows 'haint blue,' hang brooms by the entrance, and keep salt and pepper mixtures in their corners — all ways to confuse, repel, or trap these night-visiting entities that drain the life force of the living.

title: The Bell Witch
summary: Although the Bell Witch of Tennessee is one of America's most famous supernatural legends, its African American dimensions are often overlooked. Enslaved people on the Bell plantation near Adams, Tennessee, had their own interpretations of the entity that tormented the Bell family from 1817 to 1821. While white accounts describe the witch as the ghost of Kate Batts, African American oral traditions viewed the Bell Witch as a 'haint' connected to the horrors of slavery itself—a spirit born from the suffering of the enslaved on the plantation. Some accounts from formerly enslaved people describe the witch as a Boo Hag-like entity that could shed its skin and fly. The enslaved community used their own protective measures—salt, sulfur, haint blue paint, and conjure bags—to ward off the entity, often with greater success than the Bells' reliance on prayer and Christian ritual. The Bell Witch thus represents a convergence of African and European supernatural traditions on American soil.
source: Tennessee oral tradition; snip Slave narratives referencing Bell Witch; snip Drums and Shadows accounts
full_text:
The Bell Witch of Tennessee is one of America's most famous supernatural legends, and its African American dimensions are often overlooked. Enslaved people on the Bell plantation near Adams, Tennessee, had their own interpretations of the entity that tormented the Bell family from 1817 to 1821.
